body_markdown:
One of the harsh realities of playing with cars is that all them will need maintenance, and the parts and other consumables required to keep a car on the road cost money. Beyond the time and space needed to keep a car exists the expense of feeding it brake pads and rotors, bushings, fluids, and even larger parts, like water pumps. For some this can feel like death by a thousand cuts, as the small purchases tend to add up to real and very noticeable amounts of money before long. Luckily, there are ways to get deals on some of the parts a project car might need, and they don’t require any special connections or tricks. Here are six that might help your project move forward while staying on budget.


## Know Something the Seller Doesn’t


Swap meet piles like this are often the perfect place to find exactly what you need and get a great price, but it’s not guaranteed.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


This can be tricky at times, and is best leveraged at a place like a swap meet, where parts are often set out by someone who might not know exactly what they have or what it might fit. If you know what a particular piece is and what it fits but the seller is looking at a random piece of metal, it is likely you will be the one who comes out on the better end of the deal.


This means going in prepared and knowing how to ID parts without asking for help. That can require having a reference part or measuring device to have confidence that what you have in hand is actually what you think it is. I’ve been victim of my own excitement before and purchased parts that were so close to correct, but were actually for one year later, with slightly different bolt spacing. Not the worst-case scenario but still annoying.


## Go Where Other Buyers Won’t


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


If you can’t know something that other buyers or the seller don’t, another easy way to find low-hanging fruit is to get off a well-trodden path. When I was shopping for a specific set of forks for a motorcycle project, I ended up driving nearly six hours north and west from my already-northern home to what could only be described as the middle of nowhere. Sure, if you factor in my time and the cost of fuel, I probably paid near market rate, but when is the last time someone included honest math in their project car accounting?


There is no need for everything to be a road trip, either. Sourcing from a different supplier or outlet can help with this. That might mean going to a pick-n-pull that is a farther drive than most are willing to take, or it might mean you need to pick up the phone and talk to that seller who doesn’t want to email. Some people really dislike talking on the phone, but if you are willing to engage on the seller’s terms when other buyers won’t, a deal might be waiting.


## Be Kind


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Regardless of how you find or contact a seller, being courteous is the bare minimum for human interaction. Understanding that some vintage parts sellers on eBay, Marketplace, or other outlets are hobbyists rather than professional sellers is often going to yield better results than assuming you are doing them a favor by buying their wares. Asking questions is wise, but being demanding of sellers often yields less than desirable results all around. Being kind is free but can also get you a deal when done right.


## Search Far and Wide


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


If you’ve got a part number, type it into every search box you can find and even ask a local parts house. Sometimes a local parts dealer might even surprise you, since we forget that all those “new old stock” items we read about people finding are often simply sitting on shelves, and we just need to find the shelf. Dealerships clean out stock a little more regularly these days, but asking is free, so even if you don’t buy anything and get an answer of “sorry,” you have done due diligence.


## Pull Your Own


Leaving a scrap yard with a truck bed full is cheaper than other options, though not as cheap as it once was.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Not all project cars are rare beasts that require scrounging digital boneyards. Instead, there is a whole world of cars that can be fixed with a trip to a local pick-and-pull yard. The bonus of this method is that you get the practice of doing the job on a car you don’t care about, which I find makes doing the job the second time on your car a little easier.


There was a time when all of the parts I needed to keep my 1964 Corvair on the road while going back and forth to high school were found by pulling them out of the local scrap yard. That included a generator-to-alternator conversion, along with multiple other engine parts, all done for far cheaper than buying kits or parts separately online. Plus, I got to know the yard owners well enough to get some free advice.


## Bring Cash


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Negotiating is an art, and one people often think is far easier than it truly is. Regardless of your negotiation techniques, it is generally quite helpful if there is physical money changing hands. Despite our digital world, cash really still is king. The human brain loves tangible objects, and handing the seller even just one bill in exchange for something can occasionally overwhelm the need for an exact amount of cash. While some do put a little too much weight on cash offers—few people are going to shave 50%–75% off their asking price just because you said it would be cash—it is something that can help, especially when combined with other items on this list.
